title: SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models
authors: Potsawee Manakul, Adian Liusie, Mark J. F. Gales
summary: SelfCheckGPT is a method for detecting hallucinations in the output of large language models without access to the model's internal probabilities or an external database. This setting is called zero-resource, black-box detection. The method relies on the idea that if a model knows a fact, its sampled responses to the same prompt will tend to agree, whereas for facts the model has made up, the sampled responses will diverge and contradict each other. The authors evaluated the approach on GPT-3 generated passages about individuals from the WikiBio dataset, which were manually annotated for factuality. SelfCheckGPT can flag non-factual sentences and rank passages by their factuality. It outperformed grey-box baselines on sentence-level AUC-PR and on passage-level correlation.

title: FacTool: Factuality Detection in Generative AI -- A Tool Augmented Framework for Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Scenarios
authors: I-Chun Chern, Steffi Chern, Shiqi Chen, Weizhe Yuan, Kehua Feng, Chunting Zhou, Junxian He, Graham Neubig, Pengfei Liu
summary: FacTool is a framework for detecting factual errors in text generated by large language models such as ChatGPT. The paper starts from the observation that generative pre-trained models can now synthesize high-quality text. FacTool is tool augmented and is designed to work across multiple tasks and multiple domains rather than a single one. The authors evaluate it on four tasks: knowledge-based question answering, code generation, mathematical reasoning and scientific literature review. They release the code, which is linked to a ChatGPT plugin interface.

title: HaloScope: Harnessing Unlabeled LLM Generations for Hallucination Detection
authors: Xuefeng Du, Chaowei Xiao, Yixuan Li
summary: HaloScope addresses hallucination detection when labeled data is scarce. The authors point out that training a truthfulness classifier is hard because it needs labeled examples of truthful and hallucinated generations. HaloScope instead uses unlabeled LLM outputs collected after the model is deployed. It trains a binary truthfulness classifier on those unlabeled generations. An automated membership estimation score separates truthful from hallucinated generations. The approach requires no extra data collection or human annotation. The authors report that it outperforms competing methods by a significant margin.

title: Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation in Natural Language Generation
authors: Lorenz Kuhn, Yarin Gal, Sebastian Farquhar
summary: The paper proposes a way to measure uncertainty in large language models, which matters for judging when their answers to questions can be trusted. Uncertainty is hard to measure in natural language because different sentences can carry the same meaning. To address this, the authors introduce semantic entropy, which accounts for meaning-preserving variation in wording. The method is unsupervised, uses only a single model, and requires no modifications to existing models. In experiments, semantic entropy predicted model accuracy on question-answering datasets better than comparable baselines.

title: Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models
authors: Shehzaad Dhuliawala, Mojtaba Komeili, Jing Xu, Roberta Raileanu, Xian Li, Asli Celikyilmaz, Jason Weston
summary: Hallucination is when language models produce plausible but false facts. Chain-of-Verification, or CoVe, is a method in which the model first drafts an answer. It then writes verification questions to fact-check its draft. The model answers those questions separately, so that the answers are not biased by earlier responses. Finally it produces a revised response. Across tasks including list questions based on Wikidata, closed-book question answering and long-form text generation, the authors report that CoVe decreases hallucinations.

title: The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying
summary: The paper argues that the hidden-layer activations of a large language model can reveal whether a statement is true. This holds whether the statement was given to the model or generated by it. The authors train a classifier on those activations, which labels true and false statements with 71% to 83% accuracy depending on the base model. They also find that the sentence probability assigned by the model is a weaker signal of truthfulness, because it depends on sentence length and word frequency. Their conclusion is that the internal state of the model can be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements.

title: HaluEval: A Large-Scale Hallucination Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
authors: Junyi Li, Xiaoxue Cheng, Wayne Xin Zhao, Jian-Yun Nie, Ji-Rong Wen
summary: HaluEval is a benchmark for testing how well large language models recognize hallucinations, meaning content that conflicts with the source or cannot be verified against known facts. It contains a large collection of generated samples together with human-annotated hallucinated samples. The generated samples were produced with a two-step ChatGPT-based framework of sampling and filtering. The authors found that ChatGPT fabricates unverifiable information on certain topics, with about 19.5% of its responses containing hallucinations. Existing language models struggle to recognize hallucinations. Supplying external knowledge or prompting the model to reason step by step helps.

title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation
authors: Ziwei Ji, Nayeon Lee, Rita Frieske, Tiezheng Yu, Dan Su, Yan Xu, Etsuko Ishii, Yejin Bang, Delong Chen, Wenliang Dai, Ho Shu Chan, Andrea Madotto, Pascale Fung
summary: This survey reviews how neural text generation can produce unintended, inaccurate content. Hallucination hurts performance and user trust. The survey covers metrics and mitigation methods. It examines hallucination in tasks such as summarization, dialogue, question answering, data-to-text generation, machine translation and vision-language generation. It also addresses hallucination in large language models. The authors aim to support collaborative research on the problem.
